title: Inventory System
description: Design an inventory system for a multi-warehouse retailer — stock levels per location, reservations at checkout, an inventory ledger, available-to-promise, syncing with physical counts, and preventing overselling.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is an Inventory System?
blocks.text: An inventory system tracks how many units of each product (SKU) are in each warehouse or store, how many are promised to orders, and how many can still be sold. It's consulted by product pages ("In stock"), checkout (reserve units), warehouses (receive and ship), and planners (reorder). Its central job is to never sell what isn't there, without blocking sales unnecessarily.

items: Track on-hand quantity per SKU per location.
Product pages and search should show availability (in stock, low stock, out of stock) and delivery estimates.
Checkout should reserve units; cancelled or expired reservations release them; shipments decrement on-hand.
Warehouses should record receipts, transfers, and adjustments from physical counts.
Low stock should trigger reorder alerts.
Warehouse picking and robotics (see Amazon Warehouse).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: No overselling: reservations must never exceed available stock.
Availability reads are very high volume (~100k/s) and can be slightly stale; reservations must be exact.
Every change is auditable (who, why, when).
Handle flash-sale contention on hot SKUs.
**Stock record**: SKU, location, `onHand`, `reserved` (available = onHand − reserved − safety stock).
**Reservation**: order, SKU, location, quantity, status, expiry.
**Inventory movement**: an append-only ledger entry — receipt, shipment, transfer, adjustment — with reason and actor.

blocks.text: 1) Stock per location and the ledger

Each change is written as an **inventory movement** in an append-only ledger, and the **stock record** for that SKU/location is updated in the same transaction. The ledger explains every number; the stock record makes reads fast.

Product pages need "is it available near this customer?" for many SKUs at once. A **projection** of available quantities per SKU per region is maintained from stock changes (via CDC) in a cache, and turned into simple statuses. Reads never hit the transactional database.

Checkout calls **reserve** with the order lines and destination. The service picks a location (allocation) that can fulfil, increments `reserved` with a conditional update, and records a reservation with an **expiry** (e.g. 15 minutes). Payment success **confirms** it; failure or timeout **releases** it. When the warehouse ships, `onHand` and `reserved` both decrease.

Warehouses post receipts and transfers as movements. **Cycle counts** compare physical counts with the system and post adjustments with a reason. A job compares available quantity with reorder points and raises alerts.

approach.text: Read `onHand − reserved`, check it, then increment `reserved`.

challenges.text: Concurrent checkouts both see 1 available and both reserve it.

approach.text: `UPDATE stock SET reserved = reserved + :q WHERE sku = ? AND location = ? AND onHand - reserved - safety >= :q`. Zero rows updated means not enough stock; try another location.

challenges.text: A hot SKU in a flash sale serialises thousands of updates on one row.

blocks.title: Conditional update + bucketed stock for hot SKUs

approach.text: Keep the conditional update for normal SKUs. For hot SKUs, split the location's available quantity into **N buckets** (rows) and reserve from a random bucket, rebalancing buckets in the background; or gate reservations with an atomic counter in Redis and write the reservation asynchronously. **Idempotency keys** per order make retries safe, and reservation expiry guarantees abandoned carts release stock.

challenges.text: Bucketing can report "sold out" while one bucket still has units; a fallback scan of other buckets fixes this.

blocks.text: 2) How do we keep the system in sync with reality?

The physical world drifts: damaged items, mis-scans, theft. Regular **cycle counts** of a few bins per day, prioritised by value and error history, produce adjustments. **Safety stock** per SKU (held back from availability) absorbs small errors so a count discrepancy rarely causes a cancelled order. Every adjustment is a ledger movement with a reason code, so shrinkage can be analysed.
Separate the two numbers clearly: the ledger records what physically happened; availability is a business decision (on hand minus reservations minus safety stock).
3) How do we choose the location for a reservation?

Allocation considers distance to the customer (delivery promise), stock levels (avoid draining a location), and cost (splitting an order across warehouses is expensive). Start simple — nearest location that can fulfil the whole order — and fall back to splits. The availability projection is per region so product pages can promise realistic delivery dates.

quiz.question: How do we prevent two checkouts reserving the last unit?
options: A conditional update that only reserves when enough stock is available
quiz.explanation: The database enforces the stock constraint atomically.

quiz.question: Why do reservations have an expiry?
options: So abandoned checkouts release stock automatically

quiz.question: Why serve product-page availability from a separate projection?
options: Reads are huge in volume and can be slightly stale, so they shouldn't hit the transactional DB
quiz.explanation: Reservations stay exact while reads scale independently.

quiz.question: What is safety stock for?
options: Absorbing small differences between system and physical counts
quiz.explanation: Holding a few units back avoids cancelling orders over count errors.
